messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing test: org.apache.commons.collections4.IteratorUtilsTest.testCollatedIterator()
  - The test first verifies that passing a null iterator causes a NullPointerException at construction time. This is satisfied by CollatingIterator.addIterator(...) (not shown here), which throws on null iterators.
  - Then it exercises the “natural ordering” case by calling:
    Iterator<Integer> it = IteratorUtils.collatedIterator(null, collectionOdd.iterator(), collectionEven.iterator());
    and consuming it via IteratorUtils.toList(it). According to the javadoc, a null comparator should imply natural ordering.

- Implementation path:
  - IteratorUtils.collatedIterator(null, iter1, iter2) returns new CollatingIterator<>(comparator, iter1, iter2) (IteratorUtils.collatedIterator(...), lines 602–605).
  - CollatingIterator constructor stores the comparator as-is via setComparator(comp) (lines 116–121, 99–102, 224–227), so comparator remains null.
  - When the iterator is consumed, next() calls least() to determine the next smallest element (lines 247–259).
  - least() explicitly throws a NullPointerException if comparator == null (lines 365–367):
    if (comparator == null) {
        throw new NullPointerException("You must invoke setComparator() to set a comparator first.");
    }
  - This exception is thrown on the first comparison attempt, i.e., the first time next() is called, which matches the test’s failure: “an exception is thrown the first time the returned iterator is used.”

- Root cause:
  - There is a mismatch between the documented behavior (“use natural ordering when comparator is null”) and the actual behavior. IteratorUtils.collatedIterator(...) forwards a null comparator directly to CollatingIterator, and CollatingIterator.least() demands a non-null comparator and throws otherwise.
  - Thus, the null comparator is never converted to a natural-order comparator, leading to a NullPointerException during iteration instead of using natural ordering.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
